draft.title: Index laws with pronumerals
card: An index tells you how many copies of the base are multiplied together. In \(x^{5} = x \times x \times x \times x \times x\), the base is the pronumeral \(x\) and the index is 5.
Multiply
when you multiply powers with the same base, add the indices. \(x^{5} \times x^{3} = x^{8}\). Numbers in front are multiplied: \(3x^{2} \times 4x^{5} = 12x^{7}\).
Divide
when you divide powers with the same base, subtract the indices. \(x^{6} \div x^{2} = x^{4}\). Numbers in front are divided: \(12x^{7} \div 4x^{2} = 3x^{5}\).
Power of a power
multiply the indices. \((x^{2})^{3} = x^{6}\). A number in front is also raised to the power: \((2x^{2})^{3} = 8x^{6}\).
draft.remember: Multiply powers: add indices. Divide: subtract. Power of a power: multiply. Numbers in front follow normal rules. Each pronumeral is handled separately.

a.why: Multiplying powers with the same base means adding the indices: \(7 + 2 = 9\). Multiplying the indices to get \(x^{14}\) is the rule for a power of a power, not for a product.
a.clue: The bases are the same, so combine the indices by adding or subtracting.

b.why: Multiply the numbers: \(3 \times 4 = 12\). Add the indices of \(a\): \(2 + 3 = 5\). The pronumeral \(b\) only appears once, so it stays \(b\). Multiplying the indices of \(a\) gives \(a^{6}\), which is wrong.
b.clue: Deal with the numbers, then each pronumeral on its own.

proposal.title: Index laws with pronumerals
card: An index tells you how many copies of the base are multiplied together. In \(x^{5} = x \times x \times x \times x \times x\), the base is the pronumeral \(x\) and the index is 5. A pronumeral with no index shown has index 1, so \(y = y^{1}\).
Multiply

add the indices of the same base, and multiply the numbers in front: \(3x^{2} \times 4x^{5} = 12x^{7}\). Treat each pronumeral on its own: \(2x^{3}y \times 5x^{4} = 10x^{7}y\), where \(y\) appears once, so it stays \(y\).
Divide
subtract the indices of the same base. \(x^{6} \div x^{2} = x^{4}\). Numbers in front are divided: \(12x^{7} \div 4x^{2} = 3x^{5}\).
Power of a power
multiply the indices. \((x^{2})^{3} = x^{6}\). A number in front is also raised to the power: \((2x^{2})^{3} = 8x^{6}\).
proposal.remember: Multiply powers: add indices. Divide: subtract. Power of a power: multiply. Work out the numbers, then each pronumeral on its own.

a.clue: Which law covers two powers multiplied together?

b.why: Multiply the numbers: \(3 \times 4 = 12\). Add the indices of \(a\): \(2 + 3 = 5\). The pronumeral \(b\) appears only once, so it stays \(b\). Multiplying the indices of \(a\) to get \(a^{6}\) uses the power of a power rule, which is wrong here.
b.clue: Deal with the numbers, then each pronumeral on its own.
